reasons: Lake citations[] carry official '785 F.3d 1128' (F.3d, type 1), parallel '2015 FED App. 0092P', and vendor_neutral '2015 U.S. App. LEXIS 7868' + '2015 WL 2217061' — matching payload exactly.

Cached opinion header: 'UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT', 'No. 14-4050', 'Decided and Filed: May 13, 2015', file name '15a0092p.06' corroborates the FED App. 0092P parallel and 2015 year/6th Cir. court.

Opinion holds Ohio open-carry made Northrup's conduct lawful and that the two facts Bright relied on (open carry + 911 call) supplied no reasonable suspicion: 'all he ever saw was that Northrup was armed—and legally so.'

Clearly-established prong supported: 'it has long been clearly established that an officer needs evidence of criminality or dangerousness before he may detain and disarm a law-abiding citizen'; court affirmed denial of qualified immunity for the stop/disarm/handcuffing.

Home 'Terry Stops and Reasonable Suspicion' is squarely supported — the opinion turns entirely on Terry reasonable-suspicion doctrine (cites Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 21, 27; Sibron; the 'armed and dangerous' requirement).
Frontier stub frontmatter and Treatment section consistently assign the illustrative circuit-split role, pairing Northrup with United States v. Black (4th Cir.).
residual_risks: The disclosed opinion cites only accord authority (Black 4th Cir., Ubiles 3d Cir., King 10th Cir., Roch 5th Cir.); it does not itself establish a live circuit split, so the 'circuit split' characterization rests on the page's own framing / external landscape rather than the inlined opinion.

Case is a consent-search voluntariness decision refining Schneckloth v. Bustamonte (opinion: 'The Fourth Amendment test for a valid consent to search is that the consent be voluntary'), so home 'Consent Searches' with role 'Key — Progeny / Refinement' is well-grounded.
Opinion expressly rejects the Ohio per se 'free to go' rule as a refinement of totality-of-circumstances consent doctrine.

Opinion's opening holding is directly on point: 'whether the Fourth Amendment requires that a lawfully seized defendant must be advised that he is "free to go" before his consent to search will be recognized as voluntary. We hold that it does not.'
The paraphrased 'no-warning rule' accurately restates that holding.

Cached opinion confirms Rehnquist, C.J., delivered the opinion of the Court (7-Justice majority).
